# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

options.description: Derive the key from the server-verified customer context; do not accept a client-selected identity header as authority.

options.tradeoff: Works without customer authentication but conflates customers behind NAT and lets clients evade limits through IP changes.
options.description: Use the load balancer-observed source IP as the quota key.
options.holds_when: Traffic is predominantly unauthenticated and abuse prevention matters more than tenant fairness.
options.cost: Enterprise offices and proxies can share an IP; mobile or rotating clients can bypass it.

options.cost: More configuration, more Redis operations, and more failure/precedence cases.

questions.question: Should the limiter use a token bucket, allowing controlled bursts while enforcing a sustained refill rate?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Fits legitimate scripted bursts while bounding sustained creation; requires rate and burst parameters.
options.description: Maintain tokens per key, refill continuously, and charge one token per accepted operation.
options.holds_when: Enterprise integrations need bursts and the goal is sustained-load protection rather than rigid wall-clock quotas.
options.cost: Two parameters per policy and slightly more implementation complexity than fixed windows.

frames.body: tokens: `0` → refill over time → next request accepted
frames.caption: Sustained rate is bounded.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Gives a precise rolling request count but stores more timestamp state and can make bursts feel arbitrary at the boundary.
options.description: Reject when the previous rolling interval contains too many requests.
options.holds_when: The business policy is naturally expressed as an exact rolling count.
options.cost: More state and cleanup work, especially across three instances.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Easy to explain and implement but permits boundary bursts that can double effective throughput.
options.description: Count requests in discrete intervals and reset at each boundary.
options.holds_when: Simplicity and coarse quotas outweigh burst fairness and boundary accuracy.
options.cost: A client can send near the end and start of adjacent windows.

brief.how: The algorithm determines which parameters the enterprise policy must own: token bucket needs refill rate and burst capacity; window algorithms need interval and count.

evidence.note: Expensive operation and legitimate burst requirement.

questions.question: If the counter store is unreachable, should the API reject the rate-limited request instead of allowing it through?

options.label: Fail closed: reject
options.tradeoff: Preserves the database-protection invariant but can turn a Redis incident into an orders outage for every customer.
options.description: Return a service-unavailable or rate-limit response when the limiter cannot make a reliable decision.
options.preview: Redis unavailable → no quota decision → reject
options.holds_when: Preventing overload is more important than accepting orders during a limiter dependency outage.
options.cost: Requires clear client retry semantics and careful distinction from an ordinary quota rejection.

options.label: Fail open: allow
options.tradeoff: Preserves order availability but removes the only shared protection during the exact failure that may accompany overload.
options.description: On limiter-store errors, continue to the Postgres write and emit operational signals.
options.holds_when: Order availability and enterprise continuity outweigh strict protection during a short Redis outage.
options.cost: A repeat of the 40,000-order event can pass while Redis is unavailable.

frames.caption: Orders remain available, but protection is absent.

options.label: Bounded emergency fallback
options.tradeoff: Limits blast radius in both directions but adds a second limiter policy and more state/precedence to operate.
options.description: Use a conservative local emergency budget when Redis is unavailable, then recover to Redis.
options.preview: Redis unavailable → local emergency budget → allow/reject
options.holds_when: The team can own explicit degraded-mode semantics rather than choosing a single failure bias.
options.cost: More code and testing; effective behavior varies with three instances during the outage.

frames.caption: Each instance has a degraded-mode cap.

options.label: Per-customer config with named ownership
options.tradeoff: Supports legitimate variation and auditable changes but requires a source of truth and a process for approving values.
options.description: Store each customer's rate and burst policy as data; API owns semantics, and one named operational/business owner approves numbers.
options.holds_when: Enterprise contracts genuinely differ and limits must change without code redeploys.
options.cost: Needs initial defaults, config validation, auditability, and an owner to prevent unbounded exceptions.

options.label: One higher tier for all enterprise customers
options.tradeoff: Simple to operate but over- or under-provisions customers with different workloads.
options.description: Give every enterprise customer the same elevated rate and burst.
options.holds_when: Contracts and workloads are sufficiently uniform to avoid per-customer tuning.
options.cost: A single noisy enterprise customer can consume the headroom intended for the rest.

frames.caption: One tier is easy to explain.

options.label: Manual runtime exceptions owned by support
options.tradeoff: Fast for one-off incidents but weakly auditable and likely to drift from contracts.
options.description: Operators adjust individual limits as needed without a defined policy source.
options.holds_when: This is a temporary emergency process, not the steady-state design.
options.cost: Hidden policy, inconsistent treatment, and difficult incident reconstruction.

brief.how: After this choice, later rounds must settle default and enterprise parameter values, source of truth, and approval path.

evidence.note: Legitimate enterprise bursts and ownership gap.

options.description: Keep an independent limiter in each `src/server.ts` process.

questions.question: If the counter store is unreachable, should the API reject the rate-limited request instead of allowing it through?

options.label: Fail closed: reject
options.tradeoff: Preserves the database-protection invariant but can turn a Redis incident into an orders outage for every customer.
options.description: Reject when the limiter cannot make a reliable decision; use a distinct availability response rather than pretending quota was exceeded.
options.preview: Redis unavailable → no quota decision → reject

options.description: On limiter-store errors, continue to the Postgres write and emit operational signals.

options.label: Per-customer config with named ownership
options.tradeoff: Supports legitimate variation and auditable changes but requires a source of truth and an approval process.
options.description: Store each customer's rate and burst policy as data; API owns semantics, and one named operational/business owner approves values.
options.holds_when: Enterprise contracts genuinely differ and limits must change without code redeploys.
options.cost: Needs defaults, config validation, auditability, and an owner to prevent unbounded exceptions.

options.label: One higher tier for all enterprise customers
options.tradeoff: Simple to operate but over- or under-provisions customers with different workloads.
options.description: Give every enterprise customer the same elevated rate and burst.

options.cost: One noisy enterprise customer can consume headroom intended for the rest.

options.label: Manual runtime exceptions owned by support
options.tradeoff: Fast for one-off incidents but weakly auditable and likely to drift from contracts.
options.description: Operators adjust individual limits as needed without a defined policy source.
options.holds_when: This is a temporary emergency process, not the steady-state design.
options.cost: Hidden policy, inconsistent treatment, and difficult incident reconstruction.

options.holds_when: Clients can be updated or already handle standard throttling responses.
options.cost: The exact body, headers, and retry calculation become compatibility surface.

options.label: 429 with no structured contract

options.description: Return only the status or a generic response.

options.cost: Poor automation behavior and harder support diagnosis.

questions.question: Should enforcement apply only to `POST /orders`, leaving `GET /orders` unthrottled?

options.label: POST only
options.tradeoff: Protects the expensive Postgres write without adding latency or failure modes to the cheap read path.
options.description: Rate-limit the operation identified as causing cross-customer slowdown.
options.holds_when: The incident and capacity constraint are primarily order-creation writes.
options.cost: Does not protect a future expensive or abusive GET path.

options.label: Both, with separate limits
options.tradeoff: Controls total API consumption but adds policy and rollout complexity to a path currently described as cheap.
options.description: Use independent quotas for writes and reads.
options.preview:
POST → write quota
GET → read quota
options.holds_when: You want API-wide abuse control now.
options.cost: Requires a second quota and more client communication.

options.label: Both under one shared limit
options.tradeoff: Simple request count but lets cheap reads consume capacity intended to protect expensive writes.
options.description: Count all order API requests against one identity budget.
options.holds_when: All requests have comparable cost and coarse policy is intentional.
options.cost: Poor alignment with the known write bottleneck.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:3-9` identifies a 40,000-order creation burst as the incident, says POST writes to Postgres and is expensive, and says GET is cheap.
brief.what: Choose the initial endpoint scope.
brief.how: This fixes the protected resource; later rounds settle quota parameters and rollout.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Orders API] --> B{Scope}
  B --> C[POST only]
  B --> D[POST and GET]
risks: Throttling GET without evidence can break read-only integrations.
POST-only leaves future read abuse outside this change.

questions.question: Should the limiter key on an authenticated customer identity rather than trusting client IP or an arbitrary `x-customer-id` header?

options.label: Authenticated customer identity only
options.tradeoff: Matches quotas to the commercial tenant and avoids shared-NAT distortion or spoofable headers.
options.description: Derive the key from server-verified customer context.
options.holds_when: Requests have trustworthy tenant authentication before order handling.
options.cost: Requires an explicit policy for requests with no customer context.

options.label: Client IP only
options.tradeoff: Works without customer authentication but conflates customers behind NAT and allows evasion through IP changes.
options.description: Use the load-balancer-observed source IP.
options.holds_when: Traffic is mainly unauthenticated and tenant fairness is secondary.
options.cost: Enterprise proxies and shared offices distort quotas.

options.label: Customer identity plus IP
options.tradeoff: Adds a network-level guard but multiplies counters and creates more precedence and configuration cases.
options.description: Apply both a tenant quota and an IP quota.
options.holds_when: You need both tenant fairness and network-level abuse control.
options.cost: More Redis operations and more failure cases.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:12-16` lists customer header, IP, or both; it does not establish whether the header is authenticated.
brief.what: Choose the quota identity.
brief.how: This determines counter keys, enterprise policy keys, and unauthenticated handling. The recommendation assumes trusted auth context exists.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R[request] --> K{key}
  K --> C[customer]
  K --> I[IP]
  K --> B[both]
risks: Without authenticated tenant context, customer-only limiting is unsafe.
Both dimensions require a later rule for whether either exhausted quota rejects.

questions.question: Should the limiter use a token bucket, allowing controlled bursts while enforcing a sustained refill rate?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Fits legitimate scripted bursts while bounding sustained creation; requires rate and burst parameters.
options.description: Refill tokens continuously and charge one token per accepted operation.
options.holds_when: Enterprise integrations need bursts and the goal is sustained-load protection.
options.cost: Two policy parameters and more complexity than fixed windows.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Precise rolling count but stores more timestamp state and can feel arbitrary at boundaries.
options.description: Reject when the rolling interval contains too many requests.
options.holds_when: Policy is naturally an exact rolling count.
options.cost: More state and cleanup across three instances.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Easy to explain but permits boundary bursts that can nearly double effective throughput.
options.description: Count requests in discrete intervals and reset at boundaries.
options.holds_when: Simplicity outweighs burst fairness.
options.cost: Adjacent-window boundary bursts.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:8-10` says POST is expensive and about 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst; line 17 lists the algorithms.
brief.what: Choose traffic-shaping semantics.
brief.how: This determines required policy parameters: token bucket needs refill rate and burst capacity; windows need interval and count.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  T[traffic] --> A{algorithm}
  A --> F[fixed]
  A --> S[sliding]
  A --> B[token bucket]
risks: Burst capacity must be tied to Postgres capacity.
Token bucket needs later decisions on atomicity, clock, and retry timing.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster rather than per-instance memory?

options.label: Redis
options.tradeoff: Provides one quota view across all three instances; adds shared-dependency and noisy-neighbor risk.
options.description: Use namespaced Redis keys and atomic limiter operations.
options.holds_when: Redis capacity and service isolation are acceptable.
options.cost: Needs capacity review, expiration, and protection from sessions traffic.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.tradeoff: Avoids Redis dependency but multiplies effective limits and loses state on restart.
options.description: Keep an independent limiter in each server process.
options.holds_when: Redis cannot be safely used or over-admission is acceptable.
options.cost: A customer can receive roughly three budgets under round robin.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:5-9` says there are three round-robin instances and an existing Redis 7 cluster that may be used.
brief.what: Choose whether quota state is shared.
brief.how: This decides whether limits are customer-wide or per-process. Redis requires a later capacity/isolation decision.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[3 instances] --> R[Redis]
  A --> M[memory]
risks: Shared Redis creates blast radius with the sessions service.
Memory does not enforce an account-wide limit.

questions.question: If the counter store is unreachable, should the API reject the rate-limited request instead of allowing it through?

options.label: Fail closed: reject
options.tradeoff: Protects the database invariant but can turn Redis failure into an orders outage.
options.description: Reject when no reliable quota decision is possible.
options.holds_when: Preventing overload outweighs accepting orders during limiter outages.
options.cost: Needs distinct retry semantics from ordinary 429.

options.label: Fail open: allow
options.tradeoff: Preserves order availability but removes protection during a potentially overloaded dependency incident.
options.description: Bypass the limiter on store errors and emit operational signals.
options.holds_when: Availability and enterprise continuity dominate strict protection.
options.cost: The original burst can pass while Redis is unavailable.

options.label: Bounded emergency fallback
options.tradeoff: Limits both outage directions but adds a second policy and per-instance degraded-mode behavior.
options.description: Use a conservative local emergency budget while Redis is unavailable.
options.holds_when: The team can operate explicit degraded-mode semantics.
options.cost: More code, tests, and instance-dependent behavior.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:17-18` leaves counter-store failure behavior open; POST writes to Postgres and Redis serves another service.
brief.what: Choose the failure bias when the limiter cannot update its counter.
brief.how: This determines degraded-mode availability and later status, retry, alerting, and fallback rules.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R[request] --> S{store reachable?}
  S -->|yes| D[quota]
  S -->|no| F[reject or allow]
risks: A 429 for store failure can cause incorrect client backoff.
Fail-open needs detection and alerting.

questions.question: Should higher enterprise limits be explicit per-customer configuration with named ownership, rather than negotiated ad hoc in code?

options.label: Per-customer config with named ownership
options.tradeoff: Supports legitimate variation and auditability but requires a source of truth and approval process.
options.description: Store each customer's policy as data; API owns semantics and a named business/operations owner approves numbers.
options.holds_when: Enterprise workloads and contracts differ.
options.cost: Needs defaults, validation, auditability, and accountable change control.

options.label: One higher tier for every enterprise customer
options.tradeoff: Simple but over- or under-provisions customers with different workloads.
options.description: Give all enterprise customers one elevated policy.
options.holds_when: Contracts and workloads are sufficiently uniform.
options.cost: One noisy customer can consume shared headroom.

options.label: Manual runtime exceptions owned by support
options.tradeoff: Fast for one-off incidents but weakly auditable and likely to drift from contracts.
options.description: Operators adjust individual limits as needed without a policy source.
options.holds_when: Temporary emergency process only.
options.cost: Hidden policy and difficult incident reconstruction.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:10` says about 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst; line 18 asks how they get higher limits and who owns the numbers.
brief.what: Choose the enterprise policy source and ownership model.
brief.how: Later rounds settle default/enterprise values, source of truth, and approval path.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  E[enterprise] --> P{policy}
  P --> C[per-customer]
  P --> T[shared tier]
  P --> M[manual]
risks: Higher limits can recreate the incident if not tied to database capacity.
A named owner is required for exceptions or tiers.

questions.question: Should an exhausted quota return HTTP 429 with a stable JSON error body and `Retry-After` when a retry time is known?

options.label: 429 + stable JSON + Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Uses standard client semantics and gives scripted integrations actionable backoff information.
options.description: Return a machine-readable error and rate-limit metadata; use a different status for store outages if needed.
options.holds_when: Clients can handle or be updated for standard throttling.
options.cost: The body, headers, and retry calculation become compatibility surface.

options.label: 429 without structured contract
options.tradeoff: Less detail now but forces clients to parse unstable text or guess retry timing.
options.description: Return only status or generic text.
options.holds_when: No integration contract is needed.
options.cost: Poor automation and support diagnosis.

options.label: 503 for quota exhaustion
options.tradeoff: Misclassifies a normal policy decision and can trigger incorrect retry storms.
options.description: Use 503 whenever the limiter blocks a request.
options.holds_when: The implementation cannot distinguish policy rejection from dependency failure.
options.cost: Breaks standard rate-limit handling.

brief.where: `PLAN.md:19` asks what a rejected client sees; no existing error format is specified in the plan.
brief.what: Choose the ordinary quota-exhaustion response contract.
brief.how: This determines integration behavior and later rollout compatibility. Store failures may need a separate status depending on Q5.
brief.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[quota exhausted] --> R[429 structured]
  Q --> P[429 unstructured]
  Q --> S[503]
risks: Do not expose Redis details in the client body.
Retry-After must match the selected algorithm.
